Dog runs and pet turf built for a Windermere yard

Pet turf in Windermere runs $10–$18 per square foot installed, typically $12–$16, as of September 2026. Rinsing a dog run in the incorporated town draws on the Town of Windermere's own water utility, while most of the surrounding 34786 gated communities buy from Orange County Utilities instead.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Two water bills, one rinsing routine

A pet turf area never runs on an in-ground system once its heads are capped, which the state standard requires regardless of which utility serves the address. Inside town limits, that utility is the Town of Windermere itself; in Isleworth, Keene's Pointe, Summerport and most of the rest of the 34786 mailing area, it's Orange County Utilities, running a seasonal odd/even schedule with no watering between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. (who actually bills which Windermere-area address; Orange County’s current restrictions). Whichever bill arrives, a hose is what keeps a dog run clean and cool from here on.

That split matters more for a homeowner deciding on a rinse schedule than for the turf build itself, since the infill and drainage plan for a dog run stay the same on either side of the town line.

Fairway-facing runs in the golf communities

A dog run in Isleworth, Keene's Pointe or Lake Butler Sound often sits closer to a fairway or a lake view than to a fence line, since those lots were platted around the golf course and the water rather than around a typical suburban backyard. That visibility is exactly what an architectural review committee weighs before approving a change, so a pet turf submittal there benefits from a tighter, more finished-looking edge, such as a paver border, than a purely functional side-yard run would need.

Florida’s HOA-visibility statute still protects a run that's fenced and out of sight from the street or an adjacent lot, but a fairway view often removes that protection even where the fence itself is tall.

Grading a dog run toward a drain, not just away from the house

A plain lawn only needs its subgrade sloped away from the foundation, but a Windermere dog run gets graded toward a specific low point or drain instead, since rinse water and urine both need somewhere consistent to go rather than just somewhere away from the house. That drain point is also chosen to keep liquid moving away from a patio slab or pool deck edge, since concrete holds odor differently than turf does and a slab that stays damp near a dog area tends to stain over time. The one to two percent grade itself doesn't change, only the direction it's aimed and the reason behind picking that direction.

Infill goes in last, chosen for what it has to control

Infill is the final step on a Windermere dog yard build, brushed in against the grain once seams and edges are finished, and the product chosen at this stage is picked specifically for odor control rather than the ball-roll or cushioning concerns that drive infill choice on other turf projects. Zeolite or coated sand goes in at a similar rate to a standard lawn's silica sand, but the reasoning behind the choice is entirely different: which product best binds or resists whatever a dog leaves behind, not how a blade of grass looks once it's brushed upright.

Say you have a 250 sq ft run behind a Keene's Pointe pool cage

A 250 sq ft dog run behind a screened pool cage in Keene's Pointe, tucked along a side yard rather than facing the fairway, runs $10–$18 per square foot, or roughly $2,500 to $4,500 at the published range, with zeolite infill added for two dogs using the space daily. Because the run sits behind the screen and isn't visible from the golf course or the street, it's a stronger candidate for the HOA-visibility protection than a run facing open fairway would be.

An ARC submittal with the turf sample and a site sketch still goes in first if the community requires one for any exterior change, screened or not, and the irrigation head that used to water that strip gets capped at the valve box before the base goes down.

Reading a pet turf quote against a lawn quote

A Windermere pet turf quote worth comparing against a lawn bid should list backing permeability class, infill type, and base depth as separate items, since all three typically step up from a plain lawn's spec and that's where most of a pet system's added cost actually lives. A quote that just says pet turf without breaking out the deeper three- to four-inch base or the fully permeable backing leaves a homeowner unable to tell whether a lower bid is a better price or simply a lawn-grade build sold under a different name. Asking for those three lines itemized separately catches that difference before signing.

Keeping a run away from the lake setback

An in-town lot near Lake Down or Lake Butler that wants a dog run close to the water still answers to the state's 10-foot waterbody buffer the same way a plain lawn would, seawall exception included. Placing the run on the house side of that line, rather than fighting for the last few feet near the shoreline, is usually the simpler path, and it keeps the zeolite or coated-sand infill pet turf needs away from water it isn't supposed to reach anyway.

Pet owners near the water face a similar setback question in Dr. Phillips, Horizon West and Winter Garden, and this guide to keeping pet infill fresh covers the odor-control side that matters on any of these yards. Our full pet turf guide has the build spec that doesn't change from lot to lot.

The side-street swale a corner-lot run can end up inside

A Windermere corner lot commonly carries a drainage swale along its side-street frontage as well as its front one, and a dog run planned without checking that second boundary can end up partly inside a swale the state's rule flatly prohibits building turf inside, regardless of how convenient that stretch of yard looks for fencing. Because a run's footprint is usually smaller and more fixed by fence lines than an open lawn, discovering the conflict after fencing is already up means relocating the whole run rather than just pulling back one edge. Checking both frontages before staking the fence avoids that.

How often a dog yard needs rinsing

A Windermere dog run needs a hose rinse on a tighter routine than a plain family lawn, since liquid volume from daily use adds to whatever a summer storm already contributes, and letting it sit concentrates odor at the surface instead of moving it down through the base. Warm months call for the most attention, both because heat accelerates odor and because a rinse also serves as the fastest way to cool the surface before a dog goes out to play. There's no single fixed schedule that fits every household; a single dog on a small run needs less frequent attention than a multi-dog yard working the same square footage every day.

Questions people ask

Does Orange County Utilities' watering schedule affect a capped dog run?

No. Once the irrigation heads under a pet turf area are capped, which the state standard requires, neither Orange County Utilities' schedule nor the Town of Windermere's own applies to that section of yard. A hose handles rinsing instead, on whatever routine keeps ammonia odor down.

Do golf-community HOAs treat a pet run differently from a plain lawn?

Not under any published rule we found. What changes in practice is visibility: a run facing a fairway or a lake gets more scrutiny from an architectural committee than a fenced run tucked out of sight, simply because more of the community can see it.
